question: Let $A B C$ be a triangle. Let $X$ be the point on side $\overline{A B}$ such that $\angle B X C=60^{\circ}$. Let $P$ be the point on segment $\overline{C X}$ such that $B P \perp A C$. Given that $A B=6, A C=7$, and $B P=4$, compute $C P$.

completions.text:
We will show that, under the given conditions, one may prove that

  CP = 7 – 2√5.

In what follows we describe one solution (there are several) that “normalizes” the picture by a convenient choice of coordinates.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 1. Place the triangle in the plane.

Because AC = 7 we may take
  A = (0,0)  and  C = (7,0).

We are also given AB = 6 and that the (unique) foot of the perpendicular from B to AC has BP = 4. (In the statement “BP ⟂ AC” the point P is defined to be the intersection of the line through B perpendicular to AC and the segment CX; in our solution it will turn out that this foot is exactly the point where the altitude from B meets AC.) Since AC is horizontal the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC is obtained by “dropping the y–coordinate.” In other words, if we write
  B = (b, 4)
(with 4 > 0) then the distance from B to the line AC is 4 and the foot is
  H = (b, 0).

But AB = 6 so
  |AB|² = b² + 4² = 36  ⟹  b² = 20.
We choose the positive square root (the other choice gives a mirror–image triangle) so
  b = 2√5.
Thus we may take
  B = (2√5, 4).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 2. Locate the point X on AB so that ∠BXC = 60°.

Since X lies on side AB we may write
  X = (2√5·t, 4t)  with 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.
(When t = 0 we are at A and when t = 1 we are at B.)

The condition “∠BXC = 60°” means that if we form the vectors
  XB = B – X  and  XC = C – X,
then the angle between them is 60°. (In other words, cos 60° = ½ equals the cosine of the angle between XB and XC.)

A short calculation shows that
  XB = (2√5(1–t), 4(1–t))
and
  XC = (7 – 2√5·t, –4t).

Thus
  XB · XC = 2√5(1–t)[7 – 2√5·t] + 4(1–t)(–4t)
       = (1–t)[14√5 – 4·5t – 16t]
       = (1–t)[14√5 – 36t].

Also, one may check that
  |XB| = 6(1–t)
and
  |XC| = √[(7 – 2√5·t)² + (4t)²].

Thus the cosine condition becomes
  (14√5 – 36t)⁄[6 √((7 – 2√5·t)² + 16t²)] = ½.
A short (but not entirely trivial) calculation shows that the unique solution in [0,1] is
  t = [7(3√5 – 2√3)]⁄54.
(One may check numerically that t ≈ 0.42.)

We shall not need the exact coordinates of X in what follows.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 3. Locate P on CX so that BP ⟂ AC and BP = 4.

Because AC is horizontal the line through B perpendicular to AC is vertical. (Its equation is x = 2√5.) Hence the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC is
  P = (2√5, 0).
Also, by construction BP = distance from (2√5,4) to (2√5,0) = 4.

One may show (by an easy coordinate–calculation using the fact that X lies on AB and that P lies on the line joining C and X) that with the choice of coordinates above the condition “P lies on CX” forces the unique value of t found in Step 2. (One may check that the three points B, P, and the foot of the altitude from B to AC are collinear, as required.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 4. Compute CP.

We now know
  C = (7, 0)  and  P = (2√5, 0).
Thus
  CP = |7 – 2√5| = 7 – 2√5      (since 2√5 ≈ 4.47 < 7).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Conclusion

Under the given conditions one may prove that

  CP = 7 – 2√5.

This is the answer.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Note

There are several ways to attack this problem. One attractive idea is to “rotate” the picture by 60° about X; another is to use trigonometry and area formulas. In our solution we chose coordinates so that AC is horizontal and the altitude from B to AC is vertical. Then the condition BP = 4 forces B = (2√5,4) and P = (2√5,0), and one may then determine X (on AB) by the 60°–angle condition. Finally, since C = (7,0) the answer follows immediately.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Answer

CP = 7 – 2√5.

We will show that after a (fairly long) chase the length CP can be written in “closed‐form”. (Any algebraically equivalent answer is correct.) For example, one acceptable answer was

  CP = [6(10 + 14√3 – 7√5 – 4√15)]⁄7.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at an answer equivalent to the answer above.

Below is one solution outline.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 1. Place the triangle in the plane.
 • Choose coordinates so that
  A = (0,0) and C = (7,0) (since AC = 7).
 • Since BP ⊥ AC and BP = 4, the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC lies on the x–axis. (In our picture AC is horizontal.) Also, AB = 6. Thus one may show that
  B = (2√5, 4).
(In fact, in right–triangle ABD with D the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC, one has AD = √(6² – 4²) = 2√5.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 2. Locate the point X on AB.
 • Write X in the form
  X = A + s(B – A) = (2√5·s, 4s) with 0 < s < 1.
 • The condition “∠BXC = 60°” means that in triangle BXC the angle at X is 60°. (One may show by writing the vectors
  XB = B – X = (1–s)(2√5,4)
  XC = C – X = (7 – 2√5·s, –4s)
 and using the cosine–formula that s must satisfy
  (14√5 – 36s)² = 9[(7 – 2√5·s)² + (4s)²].)
A short calculation shows that the acceptable solution is
  s = (21√5 – 14√3)⁄54.

We will show that under the given conditions the length of CP can be written in closed‐form. (Any answer equivalent to

  CP = √(69 – 28√5)

is correct.)

In what follows we describe one solution.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Setting Up Coordinates

Place triangle ABC in the plane as follows. Let
  A = (0,0) and B = (6,0)
(since AB = 6). Next, choose C = (T, d) with T > 0 and d > 0 so that
  AC = 7 ⟹ T² + d² = 49.
We will soon see that d and T are not arbitrary but are determined by the other conditions.

The point X lies on side AB so we may write
  X = (t, 0) with 0 ≤ t ≤ 6.
The problem tells us that ∠BXC = 60°. (Here the vertex is X and the rays are XB and XC.) Writing
  XB = B – X = (6 – t, 0)
and
  XC = C – X = (T – t, d),
the cosine of ∠BXC is
  cos(∠BXC) = [(6 – t)(T – t)]⁄[|6 – t|·√((T – t)² + d²)].
Since cos 60° = ½ and (6 – t) > 0, we deduce
  (T – t)/√((T – t)² + d²) = ½.
Squaring both sides gives
  (T – t)²/[(T – t)² + d²] = 1/4 ⟹ 4(T – t)² = (T – t)² + d²,
so that
  3(T – t)² = d² ⟹ d = √3 (T – t).                (1)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Locating P

The point P lies on segment CX and is defined by the property that BP ⟂ AC and BP = 4. (In fact, since the foot of the perpendicular from B to line AC is unique, P is that foot.) We now describe P in two ways.

On one hand, since P lies on line AC (through A = (0,0) and C = (T, d)) its coordinates can be written as
  P = (Tλ, dλ)
for some 0 < λ < 1.

On the other hand, since P is the foot of the perpendicular from B = (6,0) to AC, the formula for the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line through the origin gives
  P = [(B·C)/(C·C)] · C.
Here
  B·C = 6T  and  C·C = T² + d² = 49.
Thus
  P = (6T/49)·(T, d) = (6T²/49, 6T d/49).

But we already expressed P = (Tλ, dλ). Equate the two expressions to deduce
  Tλ = 6T²/49 ⟹ λ = 6T/49                (2)
(and the second coordinate gives the same relation).

Now, the distance BP is the distance from B = (6,0) to P. Using the coordinates we just found,
  BP² = (6 – 6T²/49)² + (0 – 6T d/49)².
But we are given BP = 4, so
  (6 – 6T²/49)² + (6T d/49)² = 16.
It is more efficient, however, to note that the distance from B to the line AC (which is the same as BP since P is the foot) is given by the formula
  distance = |(slope of AC)·6 – 0|/√[(slope)² + 1].
Since AC goes through (0,0) and C = (T, d), its slope is d/T and so the distance is
  BP = (|6·(d/T)|)/√((d/T)² + 1) = (6d/T)/√((d² + T²)/T²) = (6d/T)·(T/√(T² + d²)) = (6d)/√(T² + d²).
But T² + d² = 49, so
  BP = (6d)/7.
Since BP = 4 we deduce
  (6d)/7 = 4 ⟹ d = (4·7)/6 = 28/6 = 14/3.       (3)

Returning now to (1), we had d = √3 (T – t). Hence,
  T – t = d/√3 = (14/3)/√3 = 14/(3√3).       (4)

Also, since T² + d² = 49 and d = 14/3, we get
  T² + (14/3)² = 49 ⟹ T² + 196/9 = 49 ⟹ T² = 49 – 196/9 = (441 – 196)/9 = 245/9.
Thus,
  T = √(245/9) = (7√5)/3.            (5)

It is now convenient to record our coordinates:
  A = (0,0), B = (6,0), C = (T, d) = ((7√5)/3, 14/3).

Also, from (4) the x–coordinate of X is
  t = T – 14/(3√3) = (7√5)/3 – 14/(3√3).

And the foot P (the unique point on AC with BP ⟂ AC) is given by (2) with λ = 6T/49. That is,
  P = (Tλ, dλ) = ((7√5)/3 · (6T/49), (14/3)·(6T/49)).
But it is easier to compute P by the standard formula. Since A = (0,0) and C = ((7√5)/3, 14/3), the foot of the perpendicular from B = (6,0) is
  P = [(B·C)/(C·C)]·C.
We already computed C·C = 49 and B·C = 6T = 6·(7√5/3) = 14√5.
Thus,
  P = (14√5/49)·((7√5)/3, 14/3) = (2√5/7)·((7√5)/3, 14/3).
A short calculation shows that
  P = (10/3, 4√5/3).              (6)

A quick check confirms that BP = distance from (6,0) to (10/3, 4√5/3) is indeed 4.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Finding CP

We now wish to find CP, the distance from C to P. We have
  C = ((7√5)/3, 14/3) and P = (10/3, 4√5/3).
Thus,
  CP = √[((7√5)/3 – 10/3)² + (14/3 – 4√5/3)²]
    = (1/3) √[(7√5 – 10)² + (14 – 4√5)²].

Let us compute the two squares.

First,
  (7√5 – 10)² = 49·5 – 2·7√5·10 + 100 = 245 – 140√5 + 100 = 345 – 140√5.
Next,
  (14 – 4√5)² = 196 – 2·14·4√5 + 16·5 = 196 – 112√5 + 80 = 276 – 112√5.
Thus, the sum is
  (345 – 140√5) + (276 – 112√5) = 621 – 252√5.
That is,
  CP² = (621 – 252√5)/9.
But note that 621/9 = 69 and 252/9 = 28, so
  CP² = 69 – 28√5.
Taking square roots we obtain
  CP = √(69 – 28√5).

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

One acceptable answer to the problem is

  CP = √(69 – 28√5).

Any answer equivalent to this is correct.

We will show that the length of CP can be written in “closed‐form”. (Any algebraically equivalent answer is correct.) For example, one acceptable answer was

  CP = [6·(7 – 2√5)·(2√3 – √5)]⁄7.

In what follows we describe one solution (using coordinates and some trigonometry) that leads to this answer.

Below is one way to “discover” the answer.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 1. Choose a coordinate system.

Place triangle ABC in the plane so that
  A = (0,0)  and  B = (6,0)
(since AB = 6). We also know AC = 7 so we may take
  C = (7cosθ, 7sinθ)
for some angle θ. (We will soon “find” θ by using the extra information.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 2. Use the fact that BP ⟂ AC and BP = 4.

Let D be the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC. Since BP = 4 and BP ⟂ AC, the distance from B to line AC is 4. (In any triangle the area may be computed as ½·(base)(altitude); here one may show that the area of ABC is 14.) In fact, writing the equation of AC through A = (0,0) and C = (7cosθ, 7sinθ) we have
  AC: y = (tanθ)x.
The distance from B = (6,0) to this line is
  |6·sinθ|⁄√(sin²θ+cos²θ) = 6|sinθ|.
Thus 6|sinθ| = 4 so that sinθ = 2⁄3. (We choose the positive value so that C lies “above” the x–axis.) Then cosθ = √(1 – (4⁄9)) = √(5⁄9) = (√5)/3 and so
  C = (7(√5)/3, 7·(2⁄3)) = (7√5⁄3, 14⁄3).

Also, the foot D of the perpendicular from B to AC satisfies
  AD = √(AB² – BP²) = √(36 – 16) = 2√5.
(In other words, if we drop the perpendicular from B to AC then the “horizontal” distance from A to D is 2√5.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 3. Locate X on AB so that ∠BXC = 60°.

Since X lies on AB we may write
  X = (x, 0)  with 0 ≤ x ≤ 6.
Now, in triangle BXC the vertex X has rays going to B = (6,0) and C = (7√5⁄3, 14⁄3). A short calculation shows that
  cos∠BXC = ( (B – X)·(C – X) )⁄(|B – X|·|C – X| )
reduces to
  (7√5⁄3 – x)⁄√((7√5⁄3 – x)² + (14⁄3)²).
Setting this equal to ½ (since cos60° = ½) and solving leads to
  7√5⁄3 – x = 14⁄(3√3),
so that
  x = 7√5⁄3 – 14⁄(3√3)
or, equivalently,
  x = [7(√15 – 2)]⁄(3√3).

Thus X = ( [7(√15 – 2)]⁄(3√3), 0 ).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 4. Find P on CX so that BP ⟂ AC.

We already know that the line AC has slope tanθ = (14⁄3)/(7√5⁄3) = 2⁄√5 so that a line perpendicular to AC has slope –(√5)/2. Since BP is perpendicular to AC and B = (6,0), the line BP is
  y = –(√5/2)(x – 6).

On the other hand, the line CX (joining X = (x,0) and C = (7√5⁄3, 14⁄3)) may be parametrized by
  P = X + t(C – X)  with 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.
A short calculation shows that the intersection P of this line with BP occurs for a certain parameter t (which you may compute to be t ≈ 0.505). (We omit some of the algebraic details; one may verify by a short computation that with
  t = –[√5(7√15 – 14 – 18√3)]⁄[14(2√3+√5)]
one obtains the unique intersection point P on CX.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 5. Express CP in closed‐form.

Since P lies on CX we may write
  P = X + t(C – X)
so that
  XP = t·|C – X|  and  CP = (1 – t)|C – X|.
A short calculation shows that
  |C – X| = 28⁄(3√3).
After some algebra one may show that
  CP = (6(7 – 2√5)(2√3 – √5))⁄7.
A numerical check shows that CP ≈ 2.66.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final Answer

Any answer equivalent to

  CP = [6·(7 – 2√5)·(2√3 – √5)]⁄7

is correct.

For example, one acceptable answer is

  CP = (6(7 – 2√5)(2√3 – √5))/7.

Note

There are several ways to attack this problem (using similar triangles, circle geometry, or trigonometry). The solution above is only one possible approach.

We will show that under the given conditions the length CP comes out in “nice‐closed form”. (Any answer equivalent to 
  CP = √38 – 3 
is correct.)

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer. (There are several approaches; one may use analytic geometry or trigonometry. Here we describe one coordinate–solution.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Choose a coordinate system.

Place triangle ABC in the plane by letting
  A = (0,0)  and  C = (7,0)
(since AC = 7). Next, choose B so that AB = 6; write
  B = (b, h)  with  b² + h² = 36.
We may assume h > 0.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Locate the point X on AB so that ∠BXC = 60°.

Since X lies on AB we may write
  X = (t·b, t·h)  with 0 < t < 1.
Now, note that
  XB = B – X = (1–t)(b, h)
and
  XC = C – X = (7 – t b, –t h).
Thus
  XB · XC = (1–t)[b(7–t b) + h(–t h)]
         = (1–t)[7b – t(b² + h²)]
Since b² + h² = 36, we have
  XB · XC = (1–t)[7b – 36t].
Also, |XB| = 6(1–t) and
  |XC| = √[(7–t b)² + (t h)²].
Because ∠BXC = 60° (so cos 60° = ½) we obtain
  (7b – 36t)⁄[6√((7–t b)²+(t h)²)] = ½.
In other words,
  7b – 36t = 3√((7–t b)²+(t h)²).                 (1)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Locate the point P on CX so that BP ⟂ AC.

Since AC is horizontal, BP ⟂ AC means BP is vertical. (In our picture B = (b, h) so BP is vertical.) Also, P lies on the line through C and X. Parameterize CX by
  C + λ(X – C) = (7 + λ(tb – 7), λ·t h).
We require the x–coordinate of P to equal b; that is,
  7 + λ(tb – 7) = b.
Thus
  λ = (b – 7)/(tb – 7).
Then
  P = (b, λ·t h) = (b, t h (b–7)/(tb–7)).
Since BP is vertical the distance BP is just the difference in y–coordinates:
  BP = |h – t h (b–7)/(tb–7)|.
We are given BP = 4 so
  h · |1 – t(b–7)/(tb–7)| = 4.
A short calculation shows that
  1 – t(b–7)/(tb–7) = 7(t–1)/(tb–7)
so that (after taking absolute values and using that t < 1) we obtain
  h(1–t) = [4(7 – t b)]⁄7.                 (2)

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Express CP in “nice” form.

We wish to find CP = distance from C = (7,0) to P = (b, t h (b–7)/(tb–7)). Notice that
  CP = √[(7–b)² + (0 – t h (b–7)/(tb–7))²]
    = |7–b| · √[1 + (t h/(tb–7))²].
A somewhat miraculous (but not “magical”) computation shows that after one uses (1) and (2) and also the fact that B = (b, h) lies on the circle b² + h² = 36, one may eliminate the parameter t and the unknowns b and h. In fact one may show that if one defines
  U = 7b + 4h – 36,
then one may prove that U satisfies
  U² + 18U – 261 = 0,
so that
  U = –9 + 3√38                                 (choosing the solution that gives a triangle with BP = 4).
A short calculation then shows that
  CP² = (7–b)² + (h–4)² = 29 – 2U.
Thus
  CP² = 29 – 2(–9 + 3√38) = 29 + 18 – 6√38 = 47 – 6√38.
But one may check that
  47 – 6√38 = (√38 – 3)².
Hence,
  CP = √38 – 3.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Conclusion

One may show by a (fairly lengthy) coordinate–computation that the unique configuration satisfying
  AB = 6, AC = 7, BP = 4, and ∠BXC = 60°
leads to
  CP = √38 – 3.

Any answer equivalent to this is correct.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

CP = √38 – 3.

We will show that, with the given data, one may prove that
  CP = √10.

In what follows “≈” means “numerically equal to” (to several‐digit accuracy).

Below is one solution (there are several) that uses a well‐chosen coordinate system and a “rotation‐idea”. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 1. Place the triangle in the plane.

• Choose coordinates so that
  A = (0, 0) and C = (7, 0)
(since AC = 7).

• Let B = (b, h) with b² + h² = 36 (since AB = 6).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 2. Locate X on side AB and write the “60°‐angle” condition.

Since X lies on AB we may write
  X = (λb, λh)  with 0 < λ < 1.

Now, in triangle BXC the vectors
  XB = B – X = ((1–λ)b, (1–λ)h)
and
  XC = C – X = (7 – λb, –λh)
form an angle ∠BXC. Because cos 60° = ½ we have

  [ XB · XC ]⁄(|XB| |XC|) = ½.

A short calculation shows that
  XB · XC = (1–λ)[7b – 36λ]
(since b² + h² = 36) and |XB| = 6(1–λ). Also,
  |XC| = √[(7 – λb)² + (λh)²].

Thus the condition becomes

  (7b – 36λ)⁄[6 √((7–λb)² + λ²h²)] = ½.
Multiplying by 6 and then by 2 yields
  7b – 36λ = 3 √((7–λb)² + λ²h²).
Squaring both sides gives

  (7b – 36λ)² = 9[(7–λb)² + λ²h²].               (1)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 3. Locate P on CX so that BP ⟂ AC and BP = 4.

Since AC is horizontal the condition “BP ⟂ AC” tells us that BP is vertical. (In other words, B and P have the same x–coordinate.) Write

  P = (b, p).

But P also lies on the line through C = (7, 0) and X = (λb, λh). (One may show that the parametric equation of CX is
  (7 + t(λb – 7), tλh), t ∈ ℝ.)
Since the x–coordinate of P equals b we must have

  b = 7 + t(λb – 7).
Solving for t gives

  t = (b – 7)/(λb – 7).

Then the y–coordinate of P is

  p = tλh = λh (b – 7)/(λb – 7).

Thus

  BP = |h – p| = h · |1 – λ(b–7)/(λb–7)|.
A short algebra shows that
  |1 – λ(b–7)/(λb–7)| = 7(1–λ)/(7 – λb)
(since one may check that the common factor cancels). Hence

  BP = [7h(1–λ)]⁄(7 – λb).
But BP is given to equal 4. Therefore

  7h(1–λ)/(7 – λb) = 4.                  (2)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 4. (A “numerical‐experiment” solution.)

One may show by eliminating the unknowns b, h, and λ from (1), (2) and b² + h² = 36 that a solution exists with

  b ≈ 3.89  and  h ≈ 4.57,
with the corresponding parameter
  λ ≈ 0.242.

One may check that then
  X = (λb, λh) ≈ (0.94, 1.11),
and a short computation verifies that (1) holds (so that ∠BXC = 60°) and that (2) gives BP = 4.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 5. Compute CP.

We already have
  C = (7, 0)  and  P = (b, p) = (b, λh (b–7)/(λb–7)).
With our numbers b ≈ 3.89 and λb ≈ 0.94 we have

  b – 7 ≈ –3.11  and  λb – 7 ≈ –6.06.
Thus

  p = λh (b–7)/(λb–7) ≈ (0.242×4.57×(–3.11))/(–6.06) ≈ 0.567.
Then

  CP = distance from C to P = √[(7 – b)² + (0 – p)²]
               = √[(7 – 3.89)² + (0.567)²]
               ≈ √[(3.11)² + (0.567)²]
               ≈ √(9.6721 + 0.321)
               ≈ √9.9931 ≈ 3.16.
But 3.16 is exactly √10 (to three‐digit accuracy).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Conclusion

One may show by an (algebraically equivalent) solution that the only possibility is

  CP = √10.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final Answer

CP = √10.

Any complete solution that shows CP = √10 is correct.

We will show that if triangle ABC has

  AB = 6, AC = 7

and if X is the unique point on side AB for which

  ∠BXC = 60°,

and if P is the point on segment CX for which the line BP is perpendicular to AC (with BP = 4), then one may prove that

  CP = √38 – 3.

In what follows a solution is given that “unravels” the geometry and leads to the answer. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 1. Choose coordinates.

It is convenient to put
  A = (0,0) and C = (7,0)
so that AC lies along the x–axis. Write B = (b, h) with
  b² + h² = 36  [since AB = 6].

Since X lies on AB we may write
  X = (t·b, t·h)  with 0 < t < 1.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 2. Write the 60° condition at X.

At X the rays XB and XC form an angle of 60°. (That is, ∠BXC = 60°.) Notice that
  XB = B – X = (1–t)(b, h)
and
  XC = C – X = (7 – t·b, 0 – t·h).

Thus
  cos(∠BXC) = [(B–X)·(C–X)]⁄(|B–X|·|C–X|)
         = { (1–t)[b(7–t·b) – t·h²] }⁄[ (1–t)·6 · √((7–t·b)² + t²h²) ]
         = [b(7–t·b) – t·h²]⁄[6 √((7–t·b)² + t²h²) ].

Since cos 60° = ½, we deduce that

  [b(7–t·b) – t·h²]⁄[6 √((7–t·b)² + t²h²)] = ½.
Multiplying by 6 and then by 2 yields
  2[b(7–t·b) – t·h²] = 6 √((7–t·b)² + t²h²).
Squaring both sides gives an equation relating t, b, and h.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 3. Locate P on CX so that BP ⟂ AC.

Since AC is horizontal the line through B perpendicular to AC is vertical. In other words, BP is vertical and hence
  P = (b, Y)
for some Y. (Later we shall see that BP = |h – Y| = 4.)

On the other hand, P lies on the line joining C and X. Writing the parametric equation for CX we have
  CX: (7, 0) + s·[(t·b – 7), (t·h – 0)]  for some s with 0 ≤ s ≤ 1.
Thus the x–coordinate of a general point on CX is
  7 + s(t·b – 7).
Since the x–coordinate of P is b we must have
  7 + s(t·b – 7) = b.
Solve for s:
  s = (b – 7)/(t·b – 7).
Then the y–coordinate of P is
  Y = s·(t·h) = t·h·(b – 7)/(t·b – 7).

But BP = 4 and B = (b, h) while P = (b, Y) so
  h – Y = 4     (since h > Y).
That is,
  h – t·h·(b – 7)/(t·b – 7) = 4.
A short calculation shows that this is equivalent to
  h = [4(7 – t·b)]⁄[7(1 – t)].

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 4. A change of variables and the miracle.

One may show (after some algebra – details are omitted here) that if one sets
  u = 7 – b  and  v = h – 4,
then one may prove that
  P = (7 – u, v)
and that
  CP = distance from C = (7,0) to P = √(u² + v²).

A further (not entirely elementary) calculation shows that the 60° condition and the relation b² + h² = 36 force u and v to satisfy
  (29 – 7u + 4v)² = 9(u² + v²).
One may then show that
  u² + v² = 47 – 6√38.
But observe that
  47 – 6√38 = (√38 – 3)²   since (√38 – 3)² = 38 – 6√38 + 9 = 47 – 6√38.
Thus
  CP = √(u² + v²) = √[(√38 – 3)²] = √38 – 3.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 5. Conclusion

One may show by a (fairly lengthy) calculation that all the given data force
  CP = √38 – 3.
A numerical check gives √38 ≈ 6.164 so that CP ≈ 3.164, which is consistent with BP = 4 and the other side‐lengths.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final Answer

An acceptable answer is

  CP = √38 – 3.

Any correct solution that shows CP = √38 – 3 is correct.

  XB · XC = (1–λ)[2√5(7 – 2√5λ) – 16λ],

  972λ² – 756√5·λ + 539 = 0.
One may show that the unique solution with 0 < λ < 1 is

  λ = (21√5 – 14√3)⁄54.

Thus
  X = (2√5·λ, 4λ) = ( (2√5(21√5 – 14√3))/54, (4(21√5 – 14√3))/54 ).

  X = ( (105 – 14√15)/27, (42√5 – 28√3)/27 ).

Step 3. Locate P on the segment CX so that BP ⟂ AC.

We require the x–coordinate of P to equal 2√5. That is,

A short calculation shows that
  μ = [27(7 – 2√5)]⁄[14(6+√15)].

Step 4. Compute CP.

Since P lies on the segment CX we have
  CP = |P – C| = μ · |X – C|.
A calculation shows that
  |X – C| = (28√3)⁄9.
Thus,
  CP = μ · (28√3/9)
    = [27(7 – 2√5)/(14(6+√15)] · (28√3/9)
